title: The Lord's dog
hook: Kabir calls himself the Lord's dog, with a chain round his neck, going where He leads (Kabir salok, ang 1368)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok, and your line, everyone else is good. Did you find your own part before you named someone else's? Today Kabir lowers himself again, this time with a smile. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

Early morning, any street. A dog trots ahead of its person, nose down, tail up, stopping at every post. Then a gentle tug on the leash, and the dog turns, without fuss, and goes the other way. It doesn't sulk. It doesn't argue. It knows whose hand is on the other end. Kabir saw that too, and he put himself in the picture. In one of his saloks he doesn't call himself a saint, or a seeker, or even a weaver. He gives himself a name, and a collar. Today: the Lord's dog.
screen: `A DOG TROTS AHEAD.` → `A GENTLE TUG.` → `IT KNOWS WHOSE HAND IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok. Kabir, I am the Lord's dog, and Moti is my name. There's a cord around my neck; wherever He pulls me, I go. Moti means pearl. It's a pet's name, the kind you'd call across a yard. So Kabir isn't only lowering himself here. He's also saying he's loved. A dog with a name belongs to someone. Calling yourself a dog was no flattering thing. And Kabir chose it anyway, with a little warmth and maybe a little humor. Yesterday he said, I am the worst of all. Today he says something close, but the feeling has shifted. It's less about faults and more about trust. A dog on a leash isn't ashamed. It's attached. Now the chain. It could sound like a prison. But listen to who's holding it, and how Kabir answers: wherever He pulls me, I go. No complaint in it. The chain is what keeps him near. Sikh teachers connect this with hukam, the Divine will, and the Gurus' call to walk in it. Not dragged, but led. There's even relief in it. A dog doesn't have to plan the whole walk. It only has to feel the next tug and follow. Kabir doesn't pretend the leash isn't there. He just knows whose hand it's in. So today's carry isn't about being bound. It's about being close enough to feel where you're being taken. Led by the chain.
screen: `I AM THE LORD'S DOG.` · `MOTI: A PEARL, A PET'S NAME.` · `WHEREVER HE PULLS ME, I GO.` · `HUKAM: NOT DRAGGED, BUT LED.` · then, large: `LED BY THE CHAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow one good lead. Settle, and breathe. Think of a small nudge you've been feeling and ignoring. Call your grandmother. Drink some water. Apologize. Go to bed earlier. Don't plan the whole walk. Just feel the tug, the next small step, and agree to it. Let your breath be easy, like a dog trotting beside someone it trusts. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let it be your yes. The bell holds the time.
Moti. The pet's name Kabir gives himself in his salok: a pearl, with a cord around his neck, going wherever the Lord pulls.
Your line: led by the chain. Today, when you feel a small good tug, a kind thing to do or a word to say, follow it before you talk yourself out of it. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs read Kabir's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and teachers use this one to speak of hukam, walking in the Divine will with trust rather than resistance.

fork.setup: you're Kabir, looking for a picture of how you walk with the Lord. what do you call yourself?
options: the Lord's dog, with a cord on my neck.
a lone traveler with a map.
fork.reveal: the Lord's dog, named Moti: wherever He pulls me, I go. lowly, and loved.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, as Kabir's salok writes it: a dog.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint insulting himself.
what it means: a named, loved dog that follows wherever its owner leads.
what a scholar hears: Sikh teachers hear hukam in it, walking in the Divine will, and the pet name Moti, pearl, turns the lowly picture tender.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Kabir, Ang 1368 ('I am the Lord's dog; Moti is my name; a cord around my neck; wherever He pulls me, I go')

notes: Salok paraphrased; confirm Ang 1368. The text has 'Ram' (the Lord) and 'jevri' (cord/rope); the index says 'chain'. Script uses 'cord' in the paraphrase and keeps 'chain' in the carry as the index requires. Confirm.
'Moti means pearl' is a word meaning, not an etymology; confirm. 'Calling yourself a dog was no flattering thing' is a cultural observation, kept soft; confirm.
Hukam and the call to walk in it (cf. Japji): confirm the connection is fairly drawn.
Gurmukhi ਕੂਤਾ as in the salok, 'KOO-taa': confirm.
Editor: 'Sikhs hear hukam' softened to 'Sikh teachers connect this with hukam' in teach, myth and trapdoor.
Audit: read clean. Keeper check: the salok's spelling is ਮੁਤੀਆ (mutiaa); 'Moti, pearl' follows the common reading, confirm it is the reading this path wants.
